subject: Russia fuel stress broadens into producer diesel/marine-fuel export suppression
body_md:
**Thesis:** Russia's refinery/fuel impairment has broadened beyond gasoline into a policy-confirmed middle-distillate constraint. On Aug. 29 the government extended through Sep. 30 the ban on direct-producer exports of diesel, marine fuel and gas oil; a broader fuel-export restriction remains in place through Jan. 31, 2027, while jet-fuel exports are separately restricted through Nov. 30. This should supersede a gasoline-only stress model with a multi-product refined-fuel state, but it does not imply imminent military or economic collapse.

**Evidence:** Reuters (Aug. 29) reports the extension and ties it to efforts to stabilize the domestic fuel market after refinery disruption: https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/russia-extends-ban-diesel-exports-until-september-30-2026-08-29/ . Russian Government primary material independently shows the pre-existing policy framework and explicit domestic-stability rationale for fuel export restrictions, including producer coverage and the separate jet-fuel ban: https://government.ru/en/docs/58316/ and https://government.ru/en/docs/58885/ . Prior Reuters reporting on Aug. 28 estimated gasoline output at ~70% of domestic summer demand after drone attacks: https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/russias-gasoline-output-drops-70-domestic-demand-late-august-after-drone-attacks-2026-08-28/ .

**Contradicting/limiting evidence:** Export bans are also a standard stabilization tool and do not prove equivalent physical shortages across every fuel product. Russia retains refining, import, substitution and repair capacity. Direct-producer diesel restrictions expire sooner than the broader non-producer/gasoline measures, so stress may prove temporary.

**Conviction:** +0.82 that Russia's fuel-system impairment is now multi-product and economically material; +0.41 that it becomes a durable strategic logistics constraint.

**First-order impact:** reduced refined-product export availability, domestic allocation priority, higher substitution/import pressure and potential regional logistics cost.

**Second-order impact:** tighter seaborne diesel/marine-fuel markets and stronger opportunity to track who captures displaced export demand, while Russian domestic transport/agriculture/industrial users compete with state priorities.

**What would falsify this:** producer export restrictions expire Sep. 30 without extension, domestic product availability normalizes, refinery output rebounds materially, or export volumes recover despite continued strikes.

**Graph transition:** `GASOLINE-SPECIFIC STRESS -> MULTI-PRODUCT REFINED-FUEL CONSTRAINT`, with separate states for gasoline, diesel/gasoil, marine fuel, and jet fuel rather than one generic 'fuel shortage' edge.
